output.query: McDonald criteria for multiple sclerosis diagnosis

results.source: Montalban X et al. Lancet Neurol. 2025;24(10):850-865
results.summary: The 2024 revision adds the optic nerve as a fifth region (periventricular, cortical/juxtacortical, infratentorial, spinal cord, optic nerve), accepts the kFLC index as an alternative to oligoclonal bands, and allows the central vein sign and paramagnetic rim lesions as supporting markers. Lesions in four or five regions establish dissemination in space without a separate test of dissemination in time; with two or three regions, dissemination in time, positive CSF or the central vein sign is needed.
results.title: Diagnosis of multiple sclerosis: 2024 revisions of the McDonald criteria

output.summary: The 2024 revision of the McDonald criteria (Montalban et al., Lancet Neurol 2025) supersedes the 2017 criteria. It adds the optic nerve region and the kFLC index; four or five involved regions establish dissemination in space without a separate test of dissemination in time. In people over 50 or with vascular risk factors, additional supporting evidence is recommended.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not diagnose MS based on non-specific white-matter lesions alone without meeting the 2024 revised McDonald criteria and excluding mimics
Do not use chronic oral corticosteroids as maintenance treatment for MS: they do not prevent relapses or disability and cause cumulative harm
Do not administer live-attenuated vaccines after initiation of B-cell depleting therapy (ocrelizumab, ofatumumab) or S1P modulators (fingolimod, ozanimod)
Do not omit spinal cord MRI in a patient with myelopathic signs even if the brain MRI alone meets DIS: cord lesions count toward DIS and separate MS from NMOSD
required_recommendations: State relapsing-remitting MS by the 2024 McDonald criteria, naming the regions that give DIS and, where needed, what gives DIT or positive CSF (here periventricular, juxtacortical and spinal cord, completed by DIT from the enhancing and non-enhancing lesions or by positive CSF, with the right optic nerve a fourth region by VEP).

Treat the relapse, which limits walking and bladder control, with methylprednisolone (IV 1 g daily for 3-5 days as an inpatient, or oral 500 mg daily for 5 days) after a urine dipstick and culture exclude a urinary infection; stop ibuprofen during the steroid course or add a proton pump inhibitor; consider plasma exchange if a severe relapse does not respond.
Offer disease-modifying therapy after diagnosis, choosing efficacy by disease activity (second attack in 14 months, enhancing brain and cervical cord lesions).

Before starting disease-modifying therapy, check HBsAg, anti-HBc, HCV and VZV IgG (HIV already non-reactive), a lymphocyte count and liver function, and give any live vaccine at least 4-6 weeks before starting.

Measure the post-void residual volume given the sensation of incomplete emptying; if it is raised, teach intermittent self-catheterisation; if it is low, offer an antimuscarinic (or mirabegron) for the urgency.

avoided_actions.rationale: EEG has no role here: he has had no seizure or encephalopathy, and EEG does not contribute to dissemination in space or time.
Head CT adds radiation without answering the question: it cannot show the demyelinating lesions that MRI characterises.
No cardiac symptom or embolic question in this myelopathy with white matter lesions; echocardiography does not inform the differential.
No palpitations, syncope or arrhythmia; cardiac monitoring has no role in the diagnostic work-up.
FDG-PET does not distinguish demyelination from its mimics and does not change the diagnosis in this typical presentation.

differential.key_features: AQP4-IgG negative by cell-based assay; both cord lesions short and partial; mild right optic nerve involvement (20/25, no RAPD); CSF-restricted oligoclonal bands; no area postrema syndrome.
MOG-IgG negative by live cell-based assay; no conus involvement or ADEM-like lesions; ovoid periventricular lesions with CSF-restricted oligoclonal bands.
B12 439 pg/mL with normal MCV; focal enhancing cord lesion rather than a symmetric dorsal column pattern; does not explain the brain lesions or the oligoclonal bands.
Normal calcium; no leptomeningeal enhancement on brain or spine MRI; no cranial neuropathy or systemic features.

differential.diagnosis: CNS lupus or other connective tissue disease
differential.key_features: Only a low-titre ANA (1:40); no rash, arthritis, oral ulcers or serositis; normal ESR, CRP and blood count.
Normal ESR and CRP, no infarcts or restricted diffusion, no systemic features.
No encephalopathy, hearing intact, no corpus callosum lesions.
No encephalopathy; second attack 14 months after the first rather than a monophasic illness; discrete ovoid lesions.

key_clinical_evidence: Current attack: two weeks of paraparesis with a band at the navel, urinary urgency with incomplete emptying, right Babinski and Lhermitte sign, with an enhancing dorsal C3-C4 cord lesion; new right colour desaturation in the same period.
Prior attack: three weeks of right hand numbness and tingling 14 months ago, attributed to carpal tunnel syndrome without testing.
DIS: 4 of 5 regions: periventricular (bilateral, left enhancing), juxtacortical (right frontal), spinal cord (C3-C4, T6-T7), optic nerve (right P100 118 ms on VEP).
With four regions no separate DIT or CSF is needed; enhancing and non-enhancing lesions coexist, and two CSF-restricted oligoclonal bands with a kFLC index of 11.9 are supportive.
AQP4-IgG and MOG-IgG negative by cell-based assay with short partial cord lesions: NMOSD and MOGAD unlikely.
Vitamin D 24 ng/mL and a low-titre ANA (1:40) do not explain multifocal CNS lesions.

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Tyrone Coleman is a 38-year-old right-handed man who presents to the hospital with a two-week history of progressive bilateral leg weakness and new urinary symptoms. He reports that approximately two weeks ago he began noticing that his legs felt heavy and stiff, particularly after climbing the stairs to his apartment. Over the ensuing days, the weakness gradually worsened to the point that he needed to hold onto the railing with both hands and pause halfway up. About ten days ago he noticed an uncomfortable band-like tightness around his waist at the level of his navel, which he initially attributed to bloating. Around the same time, he developed urinary urgency with occasional episodes of near-incontinence, requiring him to rush to the bathroom multiple times per hour. He has not had any frank urinary incontinence but describes a sensation of incomplete bladder emptying. He stopped running entirely due to his legs feeling weak and uncoordinated. He denies any back pain, recent trauma, or heavy lifting. He recalls an episode approximately 14 months ago when he developed numbness and tingling in his right hand that lasted about three weeks. He was seen at an urgent care clinic and told it was likely carpal tunnel syndrome; no imaging or nerve conduction studies were performed, and the symptoms eventually resolved spontaneously. Over the past few days, he has also noticed that his vision in the right eye seems slightly less vivid than the left, particularly for colors, though he has not had any frank vision loss or pain with eye movements. He reports increased fatigue over the past month, requiring naps after work, which is unusual for him. He denies fever, weight loss, night sweats, joint pain, skin rash, or oral ulcers. He has no recent travel history or sick contacts. He has never had an MRI or lumbar puncture. His partner urged him to come to the emergency department after he nearly fell descending the stairs yesterday evening.

neurological_exam.additional: Lhermitte sign positive — patient reports electric shock sensation radiating down spine with neck flexion. No meningismus. No Uhthoff phenomenon elicited during exam.

neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils equal, round, and reactive to light. Visual acuity 20/20 left eye, 20/25 right eye. Color desaturation noted in the right eye compared to left on red desaturation testing. Visual fields full to confrontation bilaterally. No relative afferent pupillary defect detected. Extraocular movements full, no nystagmus at primary gaze; 2-3 unsustained beats of end-point nystagmus on extreme leftward gaze. No facial asymmetry. Hearing grossly intact. Palate elevates symmetrically. Tongue midline.
neurological_exam.gait: Mildly spastic gait with reduced stride length. Circumducts slightly on the left. Tandem gait impaired — steps off line twice. Romberg positive with moderate sway, corrects without falling.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and oriented to person, place, time, and situation. Affect mildly anxious. Speech fluent without dysarthria. Language comprehension and repetition intact. Attention preserved — serial sevens performed without error. Short-term memory intact (3/3 objects at 5 minutes). No cognitive complaints aside from subjective difficulty concentrating attributed to fatigue.
neurological_exam.motor: Upper extremities: 5/5 strength bilaterally in deltoids, biceps, triceps, wrist extensors, grip, and intrinsic hand muscles. Lower extremities: 4+/5 hip flexion bilaterally, 4/5 knee extension bilaterally, 4+/5 ankle dorsiflexion bilaterally. No pronator drift. No fasciculations or atrophy.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Upper extremities: biceps 2+, triceps 2+, brachioradialis 2+ bilaterally. Lower extremities: patellar 3+ bilaterally with crossed adductor response on the left, Achilles 2+ bilaterally. Right plantar response extensor (upgoing), left plantar response equivocal.
neurological_exam.sensory: Light touch intact in upper extremities bilaterally. Reduced vibration sense at both great toes (dampened compared to ankles). Decreased light touch and pinprick sensation over the anterior thighs and medial calves bilaterally, more prominent on the left. Temperature sensation not formally tested. Proprioception intact at great toes bilaterally.
